summary: NASA and its partners are accelerating lunar lander development and outlining operational test plans for the Artemis III and IV missions, adopting an Apollo-era sense of urgency to land astronauts on the Moon within two years. In commercial launch developments, SpaceX successfully placed another batch of Starlink satellites into orbit, while Rocket Lab launched three Hawk signals intelligence satellites. Meanwhile, private lunar technology advances as the Griffin moon lander undergoes testing and preliminary research suggests everyday Mylar could serve as an effective insulator for future lunar habitats. On the defense front, the U.S. Space Force awarded its first six operational contracts for civil reserve space monitoring support, and the Department of Defense selected Orbital Operations for a cryogenic spacecraft demonstration. Orbital security remains a concern as Russia tails a Ukraine-linked U.S. satellite, prompting Kyiv to explore purchasing planned sovereign communication satellites from ICEYE and Nokia. In civil space and science news, NASA’s long-running Swift mission has officially concluded, while new astrophysical research indicates that "stupendously large" black holes do not make up a major component of dark matter and theoretical calculations suggest fast-spinning black holes could split in two. Looking ahead, space industry observers should monitor a key development on November 5 focused on satellite mission management at the edge.
